unit.title: SimpleBot: A Small Wrapper, a Real Project
unit.pitch: Build a small Python wrapper around an LLM, then handle the edges: prompts, errors, secrets, tests and classroom use.

blocks.html: A wrapper is a promise about how the rest of the program will talk to a model.
The Concept First

A raw API call is a request with a URL, headers, a JSON body and a response. That is not hard to write once. It is hard to write consistently in every script, notebook and classroom example.

A wrapper puts the call in one place. It gives the rest of the program a small, stable interface:

response = get_response("Tell me about planets")

The wrapper hides the transport details. It also makes decisions: which model, which system prompt, how long to wait, what to return when the request fails.

That is the trade. A wrapper reduces repetition and gives you one place to fix a bug. It also hides behaviour. If the wrapper is badly designed, every caller inherits the same problem.

A good wrapper is small, readable and honest about what it does. It does not pretend the model is reliable. It does not hide errors in a cheerful sentence. It does not put a secret in the source.
Understanding Through a Light Switch

A light switch hides the wiring. You press it; the light comes on. The switch is useful because the interface is small and predictable.

If the switch is wired to the wrong circuit, every room inherits the mistake. If the switch sparks, you do not blame the bulb.

A wrapper is a switch. Its job is to make the common case easy and the failure visible.
Discovering the Wrapper with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Name the Hidden Decisions

Ask the AI to list what the one-line call hides.

Here is a wrapper call:
response = get_response("Tell me about planets")

List every decision the wrapper must make for this line to work.
Include the API URL, model, system prompt, timeout, headers, response
field and error behaviour. Mark which decisions a caller might need to
override.

A good answer will separate the stable defaults from the parameters that should be configurable.

Exploration 2: Draw the Boundary

Ask what belongs inside and outside the wrapper.

The wrapper currently handles the HTTP call, model selection, system
prompt and error messages. Which of these belong inside the wrapper,
which belong in configuration, and which belong in the caller? Explain
the trade-off.

The boundary is a design decision, not a rule. The point is to make it deliberately.

Exploration 3: Find the Bad Wrapper

Ask the AI to critique a wrapper that hides too much.

A wrapper catches every exception and returns "Sorry, something went
wrong." Explain why this is a poor interface for a programming class.
What should it return or raise instead?

A silent failure teaches students that the tool is unreliable and the error is unknowable.
From Concept to Practice

A wrapper contract:

```markdown
get_response
Inputs
prompt, model, system, stream, api_url
Defaults
model, system, timeout, API URL
Returns
The model text, or a clearly labelled error.
Raises
Nothing for model-side errors; the caller gets a readable result.
Hides
HTTP method, headers, JSON shape, provider-specific fields.
Does not hide

Which model answered, whether the prompt was empty, or the fact that the call failed. ```

The contract is what another developer reads before using the function.
Code Task
Read src/simplebot/core.py. Write the contract above for the code as it exists. Then mark one thing you would change.
Business Connection

Wrappers are how teams standardise a dependency. One wrapper means one place to update the model, the provider, the timeout or the logging.

A wrapper that hides too much becomes a single point of failure. A wrapper that exposes too much is not a wrapper. The useful middle is a small interface with honest errors and configurable defaults.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 1.1 (Level 1). List three things a wrapper hides and one thing it should not hide.

Exercise 1.2 (Level 2). Write the contract for get_response.

Exercise 1.3 (Level 3). Identify one decision that should be configurable rather than hard-coded.

Exercise 1.4 (Level 4). Critique a wrapper that catches every error and returns a cheerful message.

Exercise 1.5 (Level 5). Design a wrapper for two providers without leaking provider-specific details into the caller.
Chapter Summary

• A wrapper is a small, stable interface over a raw API.
  • It hides transport and repeats decisions in one place.
  • Good wrappers are honest about errors and configurability.
  • A bad wrapper spreads one mistake to every caller.
  • The contract is the design.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Named the hidden decisions
  • [ ] Wrote the wrapper contract
  • [ ] Identified one configurable default
  • [ ] Found one thing the wrapper should not hide
  • [ ] Read the core module
Your Learning Journal

1. Which hidden decision surprised you?
  2. What would you expose to the caller?
  3. Where could a silent failure hide?
Next Steps
The wrapper has a contract. The next chapter follows the call behind it.
Between the prompt and the response there is an HTTP request you can inspect.
The Concept First

The wrapper sends a POST request to an LLM API. The request has:

  • a URL, such as a local Ollama endpoint or a hosted service
  • headers, including the content type and, where required, an API key
  • a JSON body with the model name, prompt, system instruction and stream flag
  • a timeout

The response is JSON. For a generate-style endpoint, the text is usually in a response field. The wrapper extracts it and returns a string.

The exact shape depends on the provider. Ollama's /api/generate is not the same as OpenAI's chat completions. That is why the URL, model and response field belong in one place.

A good first call is observable. Print the URL, the model and the request body. Then print the raw response before extracting the text. You cannot debug a transport you cannot see.
Understanding Through a Postal Order

You fill in an order form, put it in an envelope, address it and post it. The reply comes back in a different envelope with a reference number and the goods.

If the goods are wrong, you check the order form, the address and the reply. You do not stare at the box and guess.

The API call is the order form. The JSON is the envelope. The response field is the goods.
Discovering the Call with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Trace the Request

Ask the AI to explain each field without inventing provider details.

Here is the request body:
[paste it]

Explain each field, which value is required, which is a default and
which changes the model's behaviour. Do not assume the provider is
OpenAI or Ollama unless the URL says so.

A good answer will keep the provider boundary visible.

Exploration 2: Find the Response Field

Ask how the wrapper knows where the text is.

The API returns JSON. Explain how the wrapper finds the response text,
what happens if the field is missing, and how you would inspect the raw
response before extracting it.

A missing field should produce a clear error, not the string "None".

Exploration 3: Test a Failure

Ask what happens when the server is down.

The request times out after 120 seconds. Explain what the caller sees,
what the wrapper should log and what the student should learn from the
failure.

A timeout is information. It should be named, not hidden.
From Concept to Practice

A call record:

```markdown
Request
URL: Model: System: Prompt: Stream: Timeout:
Response

Status: Raw JSON: Extracted text: Error: ```

Keep the record for one successful and one failed call. The pair is more instructive than the success alone.
Code Task
Run one call against a local Ollama server or a test double. Print the URL, model, request body and raw response. Then run the same call with the server stopped and record the error.
Business Connection

The first call is where cost, latency and privacy enter the project. A hosted call sends the prompt to another company. A local call uses your hardware. A timeout is a user experience.

A wrapper that makes the call observable makes those trade-offs discussable.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 2.1 (Level 1). List the parts of an HTTP request.

Exercise 2.2 (Level 2). Explain the role of the system prompt.

Exercise 2.3 (Level 3). Print a request body and explain each field.

Exercise 2.4 (Level 4). Compare a successful call with a timeout.

Exercise 2.5 (Level 5). Adapt the call to a second provider without changing the caller.
Chapter Summary

• The wrapper sends an HTTP POST with a JSON body.
  • The response shape depends on the provider.
  • Print the request and the raw response before extracting text.
  • A missing field and a timeout are errors, not silence.
  • The first call is where cost, latency and privacy appear.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Traced one request
  • [ ] Identified the response field
  • [ ] Tested one failure
  • [ ] Recorded the raw response
  • [ ] Named one privacy trade-off
Your Learning Journal

1. Which field changed the output most?
  2. What did the raw response show that the extracted text hid?
  3. What should a student learn from a timeout?
Next Steps
The call works. The next chapter changes the system prompt and builds personalities.
A personality is a system prompt with a name, a purpose and a test.
The Concept First

The system prompt sets the model's standing instruction. It can change tone, role, format and constraints. It does not add knowledge the model does not have, and it does not guarantee compliance.

SimpleBot ships with a handful of personalities:

  • pirate_bot: nautical tone
  • shakespeare_bot: Early Modern English style
  • emoji_bot: mostly emojis
  • teacher_bot: patient explanation
  • coder_bot: code-focused assistance

Each personality is a small function that calls get_response with a different system string. The duplication is deliberate at this size. It is easy to read and easy to change.

The design questions:

  • What is the personality for?
  • What should it never do?
  • How would you test that it behaves?
  • When is a personality a gimmick rather than a teaching tool?

A classroom bot should make a concept clearer, not just make the output more entertaining.
Understanding Through a Costume

A costume changes how a person is perceived. It does not change what they know.

A system prompt is a costume for the model. It changes tone and framing. It does not turn a general model into a subject expert.
Discovering Personalities with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Compare Two Prompts

Ask the AI to compare a persona prompt with a task prompt.

Here are two system prompts:
[paste them]

Explain what each one changes about the response. Which one is a
personality and which one is a constraint? What could each one fail to
control?

A good answer will separate tone from task and note that a persona can introduce stereotypes.

Exploration 2: Write a Teaching Persona

Ask for a system prompt with a purpose and a limit.

Write a system prompt for a patient programming tutor. It should explain
one concept at a time, ask a checking question and refuse to write a
complete assignment for the student. Include the behaviour you would
test.

The limit is the important part. A tutor that does the homework is not a tutor.

Exploration 3: Test the Persona

Ask how to check whether it behaves.

Design three test prompts for the tutor persona: one normal question,
one request for the full answer and one confused follow-up. State the
expected behaviour for each.

A persona without a test is a hope.
From Concept to Practice

A personality record:

Field Entry
Name teacher_bot
Purpose Explain one concept at a time
System prompt Patient, clear, asks a checking question
Limit Does not complete assessed work
Test 1 Normal question gets an explanation and a question
Test 2 Full-answer request gets a refusal and a hint
Test 3 Confused follow-up gets a simpler explanation
Risk Stereotyping, over-helpfulness, false confidence

The record makes the persona reviewable.
Code Task
Add a scientist_bot to the package. Give it a purpose, a limit and three test prompts. Run the tests with a mock, not a live model.
Business Connection

Personas are used in customer service, training and internal tools. They shape tone and trust.

A persona that overclaims expertise is a liability. A persona that refuses to help is a frustration. The design is the balance between tone, capability and limits.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 3.1 (Level 1). Explain the difference between a system prompt and a user prompt.

Exercise 3.2 (Level 2). Compare two personality prompts and describe the difference.

Exercise 3.3 (Level 3). Write a teaching persona with a limit.

Exercise 3.4 (Level 4). Write three tests for the persona.

Exercise 3.5 (Level 5). Add a new personality to the package and test it without a live model.
Chapter Summary

• A personality is a system prompt with a name.
  • A system prompt changes tone and framing, not knowledge.
  • Good classroom personas have limits and tests.
  • Duplication is acceptable at a small size if it stays readable.
  • A persona without a test is a hope.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Compared a persona with a constraint
  • [ ] Wrote a teaching persona
  • [ ] Named a limit
  • [ ] Wrote three tests
  • [ ] Added or planned one new personality
Your Learning Journal

1. Which personality was most useful, and why?
  2. Where could a persona stereotype?
  3. What should a tutor refuse to do?
Next Steps
The persona changes the voice. The next chapter handles the edges: empty input, failures and timeouts.

options: The transport details and repeated decisions behind one small interface
The fact that a model was used
questions.explanation: A wrapper puts the URL, model, system prompt, timeout and error behaviour in one place.

questions.prompt: What should a wrapper not hide?
options: Whether the call failed, which model answered, and an empty prompt
questions.explanation: A silent failure teaches the caller that the result cannot be trusted or diagnosed.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the system prompt?
options: It sets a standing instruction that shapes tone, role and constraints
It stores the conversation between calls
questions.explanation: A personality is a system prompt with a name. It changes tone and framing, not knowledge.

Because functions cannot call other functions
Because it hides the system prompt

blocks.html: The happy path is the demo. The edges are the project.
The Concept First

A wrapper has three surfaces:

  • Input: what the caller sends. An empty prompt, a very long prompt, a missing model, a bad URL.
  • Output: what the provider returns. A response field, a different field, a non-JSON body, an empty string.
  • Failure: what happens when the network, the server or the response is wrong. Timeout, connection error, HTTP error, JSON error.

A good wrapper validates the cheap cases before the call, names the failure after it, and returns something the caller can act on.

The current case-study code handles an empty prompt and catches request exceptions. It returns an error string. That is a reasonable teaching choice for a small bot. It is not enough for a production tool, because the caller cannot distinguish a model answer from an error message by type.

The design decision:

  • Return a result object with text, ok and error.
  • Or raise a custom exception for failures.
  • Or return a string for the classroom and document the limitation.

Pick one and test it.
Understanding Through a Vending Machine

A vending machine accepts a coin, checks it, dispenses the item or returns the coin. It does not return a chocolate bar wrapper with "out of order" written on it.

A wrapper should not return a normal-looking string when the call failed. The caller needs to know the difference.
Discovering Failure with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: List the Edges

Ask the AI to enumerate the failure cases.

Here is the wrapper:
[paste it]

List every input, output and transport failure the function can meet.
Group them by where they happen: before the call, during the call, after
the call. For each, say what the caller should see.

A good answer will include empty input, missing model, bad URL, timeout, connection reset, HTTP 401/403/429/500, non-JSON body, missing response field and empty response.

Exploration 2: Choose the Contract

Ask for the trade-off between strings and exceptions.

The wrapper returns a string for every outcome. Compare that with a
result object and with custom exceptions. Which is best for a classroom
library, and which is best for a production service? Explain the cost of
each.

There is no universal answer. The contract should be explicit.

Exploration 3: Write the Message

Ask what a student should see.

The model server is not running. Write the error message a student
should see. It must say what failed, what to check and what to do next.
It must not pretend the model answered.

A useful message is specific: "Could not connect to the model server at the configured URL. Run ollama serve or check the API URL."
From Concept to Practice

A failure table:

Case Where Caller sees Log
Empty prompt Before Readable validation message Debug
Bad URL During Connection error with URL Warning
Timeout During Timeout message with limit Warning
HTTP 401 After Authentication error Error, no key
HTTP 429 After Rate-limit message Warning
Non-JSON After Response-format error Error, redacted body
Missing field After Response-field error Error, redacted body

The log is for the developer. The message is for the user. They are not the same text.
Code Task
Add one validation and one output check to the wrapper. Write a test for each. Do not call a live model.
Business Connection

Error handling is user experience and security. A raw exception can leak a URL, a key fragment or a stack trace. A cheerful "something went wrong" hides the cause and wastes support time.

A named failure with a safe message is the professional middle.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 4.1 (Level 1). List three input failures and three transport failures.

Exercise 4.2 (Level 2). Write a validation message for an empty prompt.

Exercise 4.3 (Level 3). Add a missing-response-field check.

Exercise 4.4 (Level 4). Compare string returns, a result object and exceptions.

Exercise 4.5 (Level 5). Write the failure table for the wrapper and implement two cases.
Chapter Summary

• A wrapper has input, output and failure surfaces.
  • Validate cheap cases before the call.
  • Name failures; do not disguise them as answers.
  • User messages and developer logs are different.
  • The contract should be explicit and tested.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Listed the edge cases
  • [ ] Chose a failure contract
  • [ ] Wrote a safe, specific message
  • [ ] Added one check
  • [ ] Wrote one test
Your Learning Journal

1. Which failure was easiest to miss?
  2. What should a student learn from an error?
  3. Where could an error leak information?
Next Steps
The edges are handled. The next chapter moves the secret out of the source.
A secret in source is not a configuration choice. It is a leak waiting for a commit.
The Concept First

A wrapper needs configuration: the API URL, the model, the timeout and, for some providers, a key.

Configuration belongs outside the code so the same code can run in different environments. A secret belongs outside the repository so it cannot be copied, screenshotted or pushed.

The usual pattern:

import os

API_URL = os.environ.get("SIMPLEBOT_API_URL", "http://localhost:11434/api/generate")
MODEL = os.environ.get("SIMPLEBOT_MODEL", "llama3")
API_KEY = os.environ.get("SIMPLEBOT_API_KEY")

Rules:

  • never commit a real key
  • never paste a key into a book, slide or chat
  • use a local .env file only if it is ignored by git
  • give the key the smallest scope that works
  • rotate a key that has been exposed
  • log the fact that a key is configured, never the key

The case-study code currently contains a hardcoded bearer token in the source. That is a real defect, not a teaching example. The token should be rotated, removed from history and moved to configuration. This book does not reproduce the value.
Understanding Through a Hotel Key Card

A hotel key card opens your room for the dates of your stay. It is not a master key, and it is not kept in the room's welcome folder.

A secret is a key card. It should be scoped, stored safely and replaced when lost.
Discovering Configuration with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Find the Secrets

Ask the AI to scan for secret-shaped values without printing them.

Review this code for hardcoded credentials, tokens or URLs. Do not echo
the values. List the file, the line and the kind of secret. Recommend
the configuration change and the rotation step.

A good answer will name the location and the fix, not reproduce the value.

Exploration 2: Design the Config

Ask for a configuration table.

Design the configuration for SimpleBot. Include the API URL, model,
timeout, key and any feature flags. For each, give the environment
variable, the default, whether it is secret and what happens when it is
missing.

A missing key should fail clearly when the provider requires one, not silently send an empty string.

Exploration 3: Test the Leak

Ask how a secret could reach the repository.

List the ways a secret can leak into a Python repository: source,
notebook, test fixture, log, screenshot, commit history, error message,
CI output, chat. For each, name the prevention.

The answer is a checklist for the project and the classroom.
From Concept to Practice

A configuration record:

Setting Variable Default Secret Missing behaviour
API URL SIMPLEBOT_API_URL local Ollama No Use default
Model SIMPLEBOT_MODEL llama3 No Use default
Timeout SIMPLEBOT_TIMEOUT 120 No Use default
API key SIMPLEBOT_API_KEY none Yes Clear error if required
Log level SIMPLEBOT_LOG_LEVEL INFO No Use default

The secret row is the one that must never appear in the README with a value.
Code Task
Move the API URL, model, timeout and key into environment variables. Remove the hardcoded credential. Add a test that the key is read from the environment and not from source. Rotate the exposed key.
Business Connection

A leaked key can spend money, expose data and break trust. It can also be scraped from public repositories in minutes.

Configuration is also portability. The same code should run against a local model in class and a hosted model in production without edits.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 5.1 (Level 1). Explain why a key should not be in source.

Exercise 5.2 (Level 2). Write the environment variable configuration for the wrapper.

Exercise 5.3 (Level 3). Find one secret-shaped value in a repository without printing it.

Exercise 5.4 (Level 4). Write the missing-key behaviour for a provider that requires one.

Exercise 5.5 (Level 5). Write the incident checklist for a key that was committed and pushed.
Chapter Summary

• Configuration belongs outside the code.
  • Secrets belong outside the repository.
  • A hardcoded key is a defect, not a shortcut.
  • Rotate an exposed key and remove it from history.
  • Log the fact of configuration, never the value.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Moved the URL, model and timeout to config
  • [ ] Moved the key to an environment variable
  • [ ] Removed the hardcoded credential
  • [ ] Planned the rotation
  • [ ] Wrote the leak checklist
Your Learning Journal

1. Where was the secret easiest to miss?
  2. What should happen when the key is missing?
  3. What would you tell a student who pasted a key?
Next Steps
The secret is out of the code. The next chapter tests the wrapper without calling a live model.
A test that needs a live model is a demo. A test that controls the response is evidence.
The Concept First

The wrapper talks to a network service. A test should not depend on that service being up, fast, free or deterministic.

The usual pattern is a mock: replace the network call with a fake that returns a chosen response. The test then checks the wrapper's logic, not the provider's availability.

The case-study tests use unittest.mock.patch to replace requests.post. They test:

  • a successful response
  • an empty prompt
  • an API error
  • a personality's system prompt
  • a custom model argument

That is a good start. It covers the contract without a network.

What the tests do not cover yet:

  • a non-JSON response
  • a missing response field
  • a timeout
  • a missing API key
  • a personality that refuses assessed work

A test suite is a map of the edges you have chosen to protect.
Understanding Through a Flight Simulator

A pilot does not learn emergency procedures by crashing a real aircraft. The simulator reproduces the instruments and the failure.

A mock is a simulator for the network. It lets you test the failure without the outage.
Discovering Tests with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: List the Contract

Ask the AI to turn the wrapper contract into test names.

Here is the wrapper contract:
[paste it]

Write one test name per behaviour and failure. Include success, empty
input, timeout, HTTP error, non-JSON, missing field and custom model.
Do not write the test bodies yet.

The names are the coverage plan.

Exploration 2: Design the Mock

Ask what the fake must return.

Design a mock for requests.post. It must support a successful JSON
response, an HTTP error and a timeout. Show the attributes and methods
the wrapper uses. Do not call a real server.

A mock that does not match the real object's interface tests the mock, not the code.

Exploration 3: Find the Missing Test

Ask what the suite would miss.

Here is the test suite:
[paste it]

What behaviour is untested? Which failure would reach a student first?
Write the missing test name and the expected result.

The first failure a student meets is the one worth testing.
From Concept to Practice

A test matrix:

Behaviour Mock Expected
Success 200, {"response": "hi"} "hi"
Empty prompt none validation message, no call
Timeout raises Timeout readable error
HTTP 401 401 response auth error, no key in message
Non-JSON invalid body format error
Missing field {} field error
Custom model 200 request used the model
Personality patched get_response system prompt contains the persona

The matrix is the contract in test form.
Code Task
Run the existing tests. Add one test for a missing response field and one for a timeout. Use mocks. Do not call a live model.
Business Connection

Tests are how a small project survives a change of provider, model or maintainer. They are also how a classroom example stays honest when the network is down.

A test suite that depends on a live service is flaky. A suite that mocks the service is fast and repeatable.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 6.1 (Level 1). Explain why a test should not call a live model.

Exercise 6.2 (Level 2). List three behaviours the current tests cover.

Exercise 6.3 (Level 3). Write a mock for a successful response.

Exercise 6.4 (Level 4). Add a test for a missing response field.

Exercise 6.5 (Level 5). Add a test for a timeout and one for a personality's limit.
Chapter Summary

• A live-model test is a demo, not a unit test.
  • Mocks replace the network and control the response.
  • Test the contract and the edges, not only the happy path.
  • The first failure a student meets is worth testing.
  • A good suite is fast, repeatable and honest.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Ran the existing tests
  • [ ] Listed the contract cases
  • [ ] Designed a mock
  • [ ] Added one missing test
  • [ ] Kept the test offline
Your Learning Journal

1. Which test was most valuable?
  2. What did the mocks hide?
  3. Which failure would a student hit first?
Next Steps
The wrapper is tested. The next chapter uses it in a classroom without teaching bad habits.

questions.prompt: Which failure belongs before the API call?
questions.explanation: Validate cheap inputs before spending a request.

questions.prompt: Why is returning a normal-looking string for every failure a weak contract?
options: The caller cannot distinguish a model answer from an error by type
questions.explanation: A result object or a custom exception makes the failure explicit.

questions.prompt: Where should an API key live?
options: In an environment variable or secret manager, never in source
questions.explanation: A secret in source is a leak waiting for a commit.

questions.prompt: What should you do with a key that was committed and pushed?
options: Rotate it, remove it from history and move it to configuration
questions.explanation: Deleting the current line does not remove it from history or from anyone who cloned it.

questions.prompt: Why should tests mock the network?
options: The tests stay fast, repeatable and independent of a live service
Mocks make the model more accurate
questions.explanation: A test that needs a live model is a demo. A controlled response is evidence.

questions.prompt: What should a test for a missing response field check?
options: A clear error, not the string None
questions.explanation: The wrapper should name the format problem.

questions.prompt: What should a failure message avoid?
options: Leaking the URL, key, stack trace or raw body
Telling the user what to check
questions.explanation: The user message and the developer log are different texts.

blocks.prompt: You are reviewing SimpleBot. You find a bearer token written directly in core.py, and the repository is public. The tests pass and the bot works. Choose your next move.

options.label: Rotate the token, move it to an environment variable, remove it from history and add a secret check
options.outcome: The exposed token stops working. The wrapper reads the key from configuration, the tests use a fake, and CI fails if a secret-shaped value appears in source.
options.feedback: A public key is compromised the moment it is pushed. Rotation comes before cleanup.

options.label: Delete the line and commit the change
options.outcome: The current file is clean. The token remains in git history and in every clone. The exposed key still works.
options.feedback: Deleting the line is not rotation. Remove it from history and replace the key.

options.label: Replace the token with a comment that says "add key here"
options.outcome: The code no longer sends a key. The hosted provider rejects the request, and the exposed token is still in history.
options.feedback: The fix is configuration plus rotation, not a comment.

options.label: Leave it because the repository is only a teaching example
options.outcome: The token remains public and spendable. A student copies it into their own project, and the exposure spreads.
options.feedback: A teaching example is still a public repository. Secrets do not become safer because the code is small.

blocks.debrief: Rotate first, then remove the secret from history, move it to configuration, add a test and a CI check, and teach the pattern.

blocks.html: A classroom bot should make a concept clearer, not make the answer cheaper.
The Concept First

SimpleBot is small enough to use in a first programming course. That is also the risk: a tool that produces answers can remove the practice the course exists to build.

A useful classroom activity has:

  • a clear learning objective
  • a task the student must still perform
  • a check the student can explain
  • a limit on what the bot may do
  • a discussion of failure and ethics

The bot can be a tutor, a role-play partner, a quiz host or a code reviewer. It should not be a ghostwriter for assessed work.

Three recipes:

  1. Quiz with feedback. The student answers; the bot gives feedback and a hint. The student still has to think.
  2. Bot conversation. Two personas discuss a topic; the student writes the prompt, evaluates the claims and corrects the record.
  3. Custom persona. The student writes a system prompt with a purpose and a limit, then tests it.

Each recipe has a discussion point: hallucination, bias, privacy or over-reliance.
Understanding Through a Language Lab

A language lab lets students practise conversation with a patient partner. The partner does not write the exam. The practice builds fluency.

A classroom bot is a language lab for ideas. It should create practice, not replace the assessment.
Discovering Classroom Use with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Design the Objective

Ask the AI to start from the learning objective.

I want students to practise explaining a programming concept in their
own words. Design a SimpleBot activity with a clear objective, a student
task, a bot limit and a checking question. Do not let the bot write the
final explanation.

The student must still produce the explanation.

Exploration 2: Find the Failure

Ask what the bot will get wrong.

The activity uses teacher_bot to give feedback on student explanations.
List the ways the feedback could be wrong, shallow or discouraging.
Write one classroom discussion question for each risk.

The discussion is part of the lesson, not an afterthought.

Exploration 3: Check the Policy

Ask what the institution requires.

The activity sends student text to a model. List the privacy,
accessibility, assessment and AI-use questions the instructor must
answer before running it. Include local versus hosted, data retention
and disclosure.

A classroom activity is also a data-processing decision.
From Concept to Practice

A classroom activity plan:

Field Entry
Objective Explain a concept in the student's own words
Student task Write the explanation, then ask for feedback
Bot role Ask one checking question, give one improvement
Limit Does not write the final explanation
Check Student revises and explains the change
Risk Hallucination, bias, over-reliance
Data Local model or approved hosted service
Disclosure Students know the bot is used

The plan is short enough to review and specific enough to run.
Code Task
Build one activity with teacher_bot. The bot must ask a question and give feedback, not produce the final answer. Test it with a mock so the activity can be demonstrated offline.
Business Connection

The same design questions apply to workplace training. A bot that answers every question creates dependence. A bot that asks a question and checks the answer builds capability.

The organisation also needs a data policy. A local model is easier to approve for sensitive material. A hosted model needs a contract and a privacy review.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 7.1 (Level 1). Name three classroom uses for SimpleBot.

Exercise 7.2 (Level 2). Write a learning objective for a bot activity.

Exercise 7.3 (Level 3). Design a quiz with feedback and a limit.

Exercise 7.4 (Level 4). Write the privacy and assessment questions for the activity.

Exercise 7.5 (Level 5). Run the activity, collect student feedback and revise the limit.
Chapter Summary

• A classroom bot should build practice, not replace it.
  • Start with the learning objective.
  • Give the bot a limit and the student a task.
  • Discuss failure, bias and privacy.
  • A classroom activity is a data decision too.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Wrote a learning objective
  • [ ] Gave the student a task
  • [ ] Gave the bot a limit
  • [ ] Wrote a checking question
  • [ ] Named one risk and one data question
Your Learning Journal

1. Which activity would you run first?
  2. Where could the bot do the learning for the student?
  3. What would you disclose to students?
Next Steps
The bot is useful. The final chapter ships it as a project someone else can install and maintain.
A small project still needs a front door, a version and a way to change.
The Concept First

Shipping a Python package means someone else can install it, import it and get the result you promised.

The minimum:

  • a pyproject.toml with the name, version, description, Python requirement, dependencies and licence
  • a README with install, quick start and one real example
  • a licence
  • a source layout that matches the package name
  • tests that run without a live model
  • a version number and a changelog

The project also needs maintenance:

  • dependency updates
  • a deprecation path for breaking changes
  • a security policy for secrets and vulnerabilities
  • a way to report a bug
  • a CI check that runs the tests and lint

A small package is not exempt from these. It is easier to keep them current while it is small.
Understanding Through a Shopfront

A shop with no sign, no opening hours and no price list is not a shop. It may have good products inside, but a customer cannot use it.

A package without a README, a version and a licence is the same. The code may work; the project is not shippable.
Discovering Shipping with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Audit the Front Door

Ask the AI to review the README and package metadata.

Here is the README and pyproject.toml:
[paste them]

List what a new user needs but cannot find: install command, quick
start, API, configuration, error behaviour, licence, version and
support. Mark anything that is stale or inconsistent.

The gap list is the release checklist.

Exploration 2: Test the Install

Ask for a clean-environment test.

Write the steps to install the package in a fresh virtual environment
and run the quick-start example. Include the expected output and the
failure modes. Do not assume the package is already installed.

A package that only works in the author's environment is not shipped.

Exploration 3: Plan the Change

Ask for a deprecation path.

The default model is changing. Write the changelog entry, the migration
note and the period before the old behaviour is removed. Include how
the package warns the user.

A breaking change without a path is a surprise.
From Concept to Practice

A release checklist:

```markdown
Release
Metadata

• [ ] Name, version, description
  • [ ] Python requirement
  • [ ] Dependencies pinned or bounded
  • [ ] Licence
Documentation

• [ ] Install
  • [ ] Quick start
  • [ ] Configuration and secrets
  • [ ] Error behaviour
  • [ ] API reference
Quality

• [ ] Tests pass offline
  • [ ] Lint passes
  • [ ] CI runs on a clean environment
  • [ ] No secrets in source or history
Release

• [ ] Version bumped
  • [ ] Changelog updated
  • [ ] Tag created
  • [ ] Package published ```

The checklist is the difference between "it works on my machine" and "someone else can use it".
Code Task
Run the package tests in a fresh virtual environment. Build the package. Install it from the built artefact and run the quick-start example against a mock or a local model.
Business Connection

A package is a dependency. The organisation needs to know who maintains it, what it sends, how it fails and how to replace it.

A clear README, a licence and a version are not decoration. They are the information a team needs before it adopts the tool.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 8.1 (Level 1). List the minimum files for a Python package.

Exercise 8.2 (Level 2). Audit the README for a missing install or quick-start step.

Exercise 8.3 (Level 3). Run the tests in a fresh environment.

Exercise 8.4 (Level 4). Write the release checklist for SimpleBot.

Exercise 8.5 (Level 5). Plan a breaking change with a changelog, warning and migration note.
Chapter Summary

• Shipping means someone else can install, import and use it.
  • A README, licence, version and tests are the minimum.
  • Maintenance includes dependencies, deprecation and security.
  • A clean-environment test is the real install test.
  • A small package still needs a front door.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Audited the README and metadata
  • [ ] Ran the tests offline
  • [ ] Tested a clean install
  • [ ] Wrote the release checklist
  • [ ] Planned one deprecation
Your Learning Journal

1. What was missing from the front door?
  2. What broke in the clean environment?
  3. What would you change first?
Next Steps
The project is shipped. The appendices collect the API reference and the classroom recipes.
